newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swissair loss narrows, sees profits.
newsitem.headline: Swissair loss narrows, sees profits.

text.p: The Swissair Group Friday reported a narrower loss in the first half of 1996 and predicted a return to profitability for the full year.

Describing 1996 as a year of transition, Swissair's chief financial officer, Georges Schorderet, said airline traffic had not been as strong as expected but the carrier would still be in the black by the end of the year.
"We will report a positive result for the full year, but our expectations will be reduced slightly based on today's view," Schorderet said in a telephone interview.

Swissair's first-half loss narrowed to 51 million Swiss francs ($42.51 million) from an 86 million franc ($71.69 million) deficit last year, helped by an improved performance by most of its units, including the core airline and catering operations.
In 1995, Swissair reported a loss of 147 million francs ($122.55 million), mainly due to restructuring charges of 340 million francs ($283.45 million).
Swissair's first-half group revenue rose 10.7 percent to 3.6 billion francs ($3 billion), boosted by recent acquisitions of duty-free business in Australia.
The duty-free activities of Britain's Allders Plc, which Swissair recently acquired, was not included in the results.
First-half losses at Swissair are normal, with the company earning the bulk of its money during the heavy business travel months of September and October.
"Swissair's results really are not that bad," said analyst Roland Leutenegger of Union Bank of Switzerland.
The result was also largely in line with markets' expectations, but Swissair stock ended the day largely unchanged after initial gains on the result.
"The size of the loss was a positive surprise. We had expected a higher loss. But the forecast is also good," a Swiss stock dealer said.

Under the new tough leadership of chief operating officer Philippe Bruggisser, Swissair has embarked on a series of cost-cutting measures to improve flight operations, but these will go into effect next year.

The aim is to improve the company's bottom line by 500 million francs ($416.84 million) by 1998, including 100 million francs ($83.36 million) in personnel costs that also will be achieved by reducing jobs.
